top.line: A proposal: let your LLM interview you about your path, to connect your own dots backwards.
top.para: Founders should do now what the book's chapter describes: look back at their path with an LLM interviewing them. Most paths are not linear, and the retold success stories hide the experiments that made people. The interview finds side roads, misread doors and what memory rewrote, answers impostor syndrome with facts, and may find a startup in an old passion.

in-short.line: Seven lines: do it now, let the LLM interview you, non-linear paths, side roads, doors, memory, startups.
in-short.para: Connect your dots backwards as a founder, today, with your LLM asking one question at a time. Paths are rarely linear and success stories are tidied up. The side roads often made the person. Look at which doors you misread, check what memory rewrote, and look for the startup in an old passion.

why.line: Jobs said you can only connect the dots looking backwards; founders should do it for themselves, now.
why.para: The book's chapter takes its name from Steve Jobs's 2005 Stanford address, where a calligraphy class came back as the Macintosh's typography. I propose that founders do the exercise deliberately and soon, because looking back honestly, with help, shows what you cannot see while walking the path.

not-linear.line: Most paths are not linear, and the success stories we see were often tidied up.
not-linear.para: My path ran from the ZX Spectrum to security, boards, news and vaults, none planned. Success stories are retold with the challenges glossed over, giving a false picture of straight lines. The experiments that sound silly often made the person, which is why I looked at what else candidates had done.

interview.line: Let your LLM interview you, in seven stages, one question at a time, in your words.
interview.para: Not a CV but a conversation: the timeline; the side roads; the doors; what each dot taught you; the connections the interviewer proposes and you confirm; what is remembered and what is evidenced; and where a startup may be hiding.

doors.line: The doors we misread: two-way doors that felt one-way, and one-way doors that felt small.
doors.para: Bezos split decisions into one-way doors, hard to undo, and two-way doors, easy to undo. Looking back, the interesting ones were misread: the job you were afraid to leave, which fear kept you in too long, and the side project that set the path unnoticed. Knowing yours helps you read the next one.

memory.line: Memory rewrites itself, so the interview asks what you can evidence.
memory.para: Every recollection changes a memory a little; research on reconsolidation, from Nader, Schafe and LeDoux in 2000, shows recalled fear memories must be stored again. The science is narrower than the everyday version. The interview marks each dot remembered or evidenced, by an email, a post, a repository or a CV.

impostor.line: Impostor syndrome, answered with facts rather than reassurance.
impostor.para: Clance and Imes named the imposter phenomenon in 1978: a sense of intellectual phoniness in people who are successful by outside measures. We remember failures sharply and progress vaguely. A written timeline, side roads and evidence are harder to argue with than a pep talk, including by yourself.

startup.line: Look at the side roads again: an old passion that did not work out may be worth trying now.
startup.para: Things you were passionate about failed for reasons that may have changed: technology, money, readiness, the market. Some are jobs that never scaled, known from the inside. The startups.sgit.ai finder helps you pick a thread and ship it; the look-back interview finds the threads.

prompt.line: The prompt, first version, to paste into Claude or ChatGPT.
prompt.para: It runs the seven stages one question at a time, notes each answer for correction, uses my words, asks for failures as much as successes, does not flatter or invent, and ends with a record: timeline, side roads, doors, connections, evidence marks, three startup threads and one honest paragraph.

toolkit.line: Next: a mini toolkit beside the startups finder, with the interview as data and a record.
toolkit.para: The prompt should become the same shape as the finder on startups.sgit.ai: stages and questions with reasons, the prompt, and a record template, so results can be compared and redone in a year. That is the proposal for that site.

limits.line: Not therapy; the LLM can be wrong; the science is narrower; the prompt is untested.
limits.para: It is a structured look back, not therapy. Connections are confirmed or rejected by you. Reconsolidation research concerns recalled fear memories. The impostor phenomenon is a description, not a diagnosis. The prompt has not been tested with founders, and my own dots are from memory, as the book says.

sources.line: A voice memo, the book's chapter, Jobs, Bezos, Nader and colleagues, Clance and Imes, and the finder.
sources.para: A voice memo of 21 October 2026; the book's chapter Connect the dots backwards and its quote from Jobs's 2005 address; Bezos's 2015 shareholder letter; the 2000 Nature paper on reconsolidation; the 1978 impostor phenomenon paper; and startups.sgit.ai, with related newsroom articles.
